A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the marine fauna of the Itarare Group is not a relict fauna of the Late Carboniferous, but a fauna that was able to survive the glacial conditions of the Late Carbonifero–Early Permian, and that the fauna of the Itara Group is not a unique fauna, but part of a trans-Gondwanic fauna that was able, at least in part, to cross the proto-rift system that existed in the Late Carboniferious–Early Permian.
the Itararè Group is a post-glacial marine succession deposited during the late Asselian–Sakmarian, with the upper portion being correlated with the Eurydema fauna.

the Eurydesm–Lyonia fauna is an early Permian (Asselian–early Sakamarian) trans-Gondwanic marine fauna that was widely distributed in the Parana Basin (Brazil), Sauce Grand-Colorado (Argentina) and Huab (Namibia) basins, as well as in the Carnavon Basin, and possibly in the Perth Basin (Australia), and in the Cimmerian area (Indonesia).
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Itararè Group, which has been traditionally regarded as a continental succession, is in fact, a marine one, and its uppermost portion (Teixeira Soares, Mafra, and Butia formations) should be correlated with the Bonete Formation of the Sauce Grande-Colorado Group, Argentina, and the Huab (Dwyka) Formation of the Hardap Group (Namibia), which are both marine.

, in addition to the well-documented biocorrelation between the Parana and Colorado basins, the Eurydesm–Lyonia fauna was widespread in the Early Permian in Gondwana and that the Parana Basin was not isolated from other Gondwanan marine basins during the Late Paleozoice.
